items.name: git-guardrails-claude-code
items.author: vinvcn
items.description: Stop Claude Code from accidentally running destructive git commands like force-push, reset --hard or clean.
items.summary: The git-guardrails-claude-code skill sets up a PreToolUse hook that intercepts and blocks dangerous git commands before Claude executes them. Blocked patterns include all git push variants including force, git reset --hard, git clean -f and -fd, git branch -D, and git checkout dot or git restore dot. Setup asks project versus global scope, copies block-dangerous-git.sh to .claude/hooks with chmod plus x, and merges hook config into .claude/settings.json or global settings without overwriting existing hooks. Blocked commands return exit code 2 with stderr message that Claude lacks permission. Customization step allows adding or removing blocked patterns in the copied script. Verification pipes sample JSON tool_input for git push through the script expecting BLOCKED output. Use when preventing destructive git operations, adding git safety hooks, or blocking git push and reset in Claude Code environments.
highlights: PreToolUse Bash hook blocks push, reset --hard, clean, branch -D, checkout dot.
Project or global scope via .claude/settings.json hook merge.
Copies block-dangerous-git.sh with chmod plus x to hooks directory.

items.name: address-sanitizer
items.author: trailofbits
items.description: Automatically detect memory corruption bugs that arise from unsafe address handling in compiled code.
items.summary: AddressSanitizer (ASan) is a compile-time memory error detection tool that instruments C/C++ binaries to catch buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-free, and memory leak bugs during fuzzing and testing. Developers enable it via the `-fsanitize=address` compiler flag and configure behavior with `ASAN_OPTIONS` environment variables. ASan maps virtual memory to track allocation state, delivering detailed error reports with stack traces and allocation/deallocation context. It integrates with libFuzzer, AFL++, cargo-fuzz, and honggfuzz; however, it incurs 2-4x performance overhead and requires unlimited memory limits (`-rss_limit_mb=0` or `-m none`). Best suited for C/C++ and Rust unsafe code testing; skip for production deployments and safe-language-only projects. Compile with `-fsanitize=address -g` flag to instrument memory operations and track allocations. Detects buffer overflows, use-after-free, double-free, and memory leaks at runtime. Requires disabling fuzzer memory limits (`-rss_limit_mb=0` libFuzzer, `-m none` AFL++) due to 20TB virtual memory mapping.

items.summary: influence-psychology is a Wondelai MIT reference skill applying Cialdini-style ethical persuasion to product design, copy, and sales surfaces. It scores persuasive elements 0-10 against seven principles: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, and unity. Each principle includes why it works, product application tables, copy patterns, and explicit ethical boundaries against fabrication or manipulation. Reciprocity covers free trials and value-first content; commitment uses micro-yeses and public goal setting; social proof distinguishes wisdom of crowds, friends, experts, and certifications; authority maps credentials, experience, and strategic weakness admission; liking targets brand voice and empathy; scarcity distinguishes real inventory limits from fake countdowns; unity frames shared identity beyond similarity. Developers reach for influence-psychology when designing testimonial sections, urgency messaging, onboarding commitments, or trust signals on landing pages where conversion depends on credible persuasion rather than dark patterns.
highlights: Covers seven influence principles with product tables, copy patterns, and ethical boundary callouts.
Scores persuasive elements 0-10 with concrete improvements needed to reach full adherence.
Maps social proof types: crowds, friends, experts, celebrity, certification, and user success stories.
Documents authority sources including credentials, experience, associations, content, and transparency.
Distinguishes ethical scarcity from fake timers, artificial limits, and pressure on vulnerable users.
